strengths: Principled and training-free formulation: The paper presents a sound post-hoc framework to endow deterministic pre-trained vision-language models (e.g., CLIP, SigLIP) with uncertainty estimates without altering model architectures or requiring end-to-end retraining.

Analytical uncertainty propagation: The analytical moment approximation for cosine similarities between Gaussian-distributed feature embeddings is elegant and enables fast, sampling-free evaluation for zero-shot classification and active learning.

Broad empirical validation: The method is evaluated across multiple downstream tasks, demonstrating consistent improvements in expected calibration error (ECE) and negative log predictive density (NLPD) on zero-shot benchmarks, as well as clear sample-efficiency gains in active few-shot fine-tuning across domain-shift benchmarks (OfficeHome, ImageNet-R/Sketch).
Clarity and completeness: The paper is well-written with thorough mathematical derivations for both InfoNCE and SigLIP objectives in the appendix.
weaknesses: Heuristic nature of the moment approximations: The derivation of the expected cosine similarity (Eq. 11/Eq. 58) applies Jensen's inequality to the denominator and factors the expectation of a quotient into the quotient of expectations without formal error bounds or thorough theoretical characterization of the approximation bias.

Reliance on pre-training data access and proxy tuning: Although framed as post-hoc, calculating the Kronecker-factored GGN requires hundreds of thousands of paired image-text samples from the pre-training distribution (LAION-400M), which is often unavailable for proprietary or closed-source VLMs. Furthermore, tuning the pseudo-data count hyperparameter $\tau$ requires a labeled proxy validation set, which slightly deviates from a purely unsupervised/zero-shot setup.

Mixed calibration improvements under dataset mismatch: On SigLIP (Table 2), where LAION was used as a proxy pre-training dataset, BayesVLM yields higher ECE than vanilla SigLIP on certain benchmarks (e.g., Food-101 and Flowers-102), highlighting sensitivity to the distribution used for Hessian estimation.

strengths: Principled and lightweight approach: Proposes a training-free, post-hoc Laplace approximation over the projection layers of pre-trained vision-language models (CLIP and SigLIP), avoiding the expensive re-training or dedicated adapter training required by existing probabilistic VLM methods.

Analytical uncertainty propagation: Derives closed-form moment approximations (mean and variance) for cosine similarities between Gaussian-distributed embeddings, enabling efficient sampling-free uncertainty estimation and probit-based classification.

Comprehensive downstream evaluation: Evaluates both zero-shot calibration (ECE, NLPD, Accuracy) across diverse benchmarks and active learning under domain shift (OfficeHome, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-Sketch) with BALD and EPIG acquisition functions.
Clear presentation and thorough mathematical derivations detailed in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: Approximation rigor: In Eq. (11) and Eq. (58), the denominator approximation relies on $\mathbb{E}[\|x\|] \le \sqrt{\mathbb{E}[\|x\|^2]}$, which stems from Jensen's inequality (concavity of the square root) rather than the triangle inequality as stated in the text. Furthermore, approximating $\mathbb{E}[A/B] \approx \mathbb{E}[A]/\mathbb{E}[B]$ is a first-order heuristic that should be formally justified or ablated against higher-order Taylor expansions.

Reliance on pre-training data: Estimating the GGN/Hessian requires access to substantial pre-training pairs (30k–300k samples). When the pre-training data is unavailable (as demonstrated with SigLIP evaluated using LAION), the domain mismatch can impair performance, leading to higher ECE on some datasets (e.g., Flowers-102 and Food-101 in Table 2).

Missing active learning baselines: In the active learning benchmark, the comparison focuses on basic heuristics (random and entropy sampling). Comparing against established deep active learning baselines (e.g., BADGE, Core-set) or specialized VLM active learning techniques (e.g., Active Prompt Learning) would significantly strengthen the empirical findings.

Scope of model architectures: The empirical validation is restricted to base/huge variants of CLIP and SigLIP on classification tasks; extending or discussing the feasibility for autoregressive/generative vision-language models remains open.

strengths: Principled and practical formulation: The paper presents an elegant, training-free, post-hoc Bayesian framework (BayesVLM) for vision-language models by combining a last-layer Kronecker-factored Laplace approximation with analytical moment propagation for cosine similarities.

Sound mathematical derivations: The closed-form approximations for the mean and variance of cosine similarities between Gaussian-distributed embeddings (and corresponding loss Hessians for InfoNCE and SigLIP) are clearly derived and provide an efficient, sampling-free mechanism to propagate uncertainty to downstream classification.

Comprehensive downstream evaluation: The method is validated on both zero-shot calibration (measuring ACC, NLPD, and ECE across multiple datasets) and active learning / few-shot adaptation tasks (using BALD and EPIG with targeted k-NN selection) across multiple architectures (CLIP and SigLIP).
weaknesses: Reliance on pre-training data: Estimating the GGN/Hessian factors requires access to large-scale pre-training data (e.g., LAION subsets). As shown in the SigLIP experiments where LAION is used as a proxy, dataset mismatch degrades Hessian estimation and calibration performance (e.g., worse ECE than vanilla SigLIP on Flowers-102 and Food-101).

Scope limited to last-layer projection: Applying the Laplace approximation strictly to the linear projection matrices (P and Q) restricts uncertainty quantification to the final linear layer, leaving the vast majority of the transformer backbone deterministic and potentially underestimating epistemic uncertainty.

Anomalous temperature scaling baseline for SigLIP: In Table 2, temperature scaling yields severely degraded ECE values (e.g., >60% on Flowers-102 and Food-101). This suggests issues with how temperature tuning was conducted on the ImageNet proxy for SigLIP, weakening the credibility of that comparison.

Approximation heuristics: The derivation relies on several simplifying assumptions (e.g., diagonal covariance, bounding $E[\|x\|]$ via moment approximations/triangle inequality) without formal error bounds or thorough empirical characterization of when these approximations break down under higher dimensions or severe covariance structure.

strengths: Principled and practical framework: The paper introduces a well-motivated, post-hoc Bayesian approach (BayesVLM) to uncertainty quantification in vision-language models without requiring retraining or auxiliary adapter networks.

Novel analytical formulation (ProbCosine): Deriving an analytical approximation for the distribution (mean and variance) over cosine similarities between Gaussian-distributed embeddings is theoretically interesting and eliminates the need for expensive Monte Carlo sampling during inference.

Negligible computational overhead: As demonstrated in Table 7 and Table 8, BayesVLM introduces minimal computational overhead (<5% latency increase, minimal GFLOPs increase) compared to test-time adaptation (TTA) methods which increase compute by orders of magnitude.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The authors validate the method across multiple architectures (OpenCLIP ViT-B-32, ViT-L-14, SigLIP-B-16, ViT-Huge), seven benchmark datasets, two existing probabilistic models (ProLIP, PCME++), and active learning scenarios.

High quality of writing and derivations: The paper is clearly structured and well-written, with thorough and clear mathematical derivations for both InfoNCE and SigLIP objectives provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Approximation heuristics in ProbCosine: In Eq. (7) and Eq. (52)-(55), approximating $\mathbb{E}[g^\top h / (\|g\|\|h\|)]$ as $\mathbb{E}[g^\top h] / (\mathbb{E}[\|g\|]\mathbb{E}[\|h\|])$ assumes independence between numerator and denominator, and the denominator expectation uses a Jensen-type/triangle inequality bound. While Figure 9 empirically validates this against KDE, discussing the theoretical impact of these approximations would strengthen the paper.

Sub-network scope: Applying the Laplace approximation strictly to the linear projection matrices ($P$ and $Q$) restricts uncertainty capture to the final linear space, omitting epistemic uncertainty accumulated in the deep encoder backbones.

Sensitivity to training data mismatch: As observed in the SigLIP experiments, when the pre-training dataset is unavailable/closed-source and LAION-400M is used as a proxy to compute the Hessian, the optimal pseudo-data count $\tau$ becomes very large, collapsing the posterior closer to the MAP solution and diminishing calibration gains.

Active learning baseline comparisons: While comparisons with random selection and entropy-based heuristics (with/without targeted selection) are provided, comparisons against existing VLM-specific active learning methods (such as active prompt learning, e.g., Bang et al., 2024) would further clarify the method's standing in downstream applications.

strengths: Principled and practical formulation: The paper tackles a significant challenge in modern vision-language modeling—capturing epistemic uncertainty post-hoc without retraining, architectural changes, or expensive fine-tuning.

Efficient analytical approximation (ProbCosine): Deriving closed-form approximations for the first and second moments of the cosine similarity between Gaussian-distributed embeddings enables fast uncertainty propagation without relying on costly Monte Carlo sampling.

Minimal computational overhead: Inference latency increases by less than 5% on base models and less than 1% on huge models compared to deterministic inference, which is drastically more efficient than test-time adaptation (TTA) baselines.

Broad empirical validation: The framework is evaluated across multiple architectures (CLIP ViT-B/32, ViT-L/14, SigLIP-B/16) and existing probabilistic embeddings (ProLIP, PCME++), consistently demonstrating improved calibration (ECE, NLPD) and competitive zero-shot accuracy.

Effective downstream utility: Demonstrates clear downstream benefits in active learning (via BALD and EPIG), showing that the extracted post-hoc uncertainties guide informative data selection across domain adaptation benchmarks (OfficeHome, ImageNet-R/Sketch).
weaknesses: Restriction to linear projection layers: The Laplace approximation is applied solely to the final linear projection matrices ($P$ and $Q$) of the encoders. While computationally necessary, this subnetwork approximation may underestimate epistemic uncertainty originating from deeper transformer representations.

Dependence on pre-training data: Estimating the Hessian factors requires access to the pre-training dataset (or an aligned proxy dataset like LAION-400M). As demonstrated in the SigLIP experiments, distribution mismatch between the proxy data and pre-training data can necessitate large $\tau$ regularizers that pull the posterior towards the MAP estimate, dampening the gains.

Heuristic assumptions in ProbCosine derivation: The moment derivations in Equations (7)–(8) assume independence between the numerator ($g^\top h$) and denominator (product of norms) and substitute an upper bound via the triangle inequality for $\mathbb{E}[\|x\|]$. While empirically validated in Section F.1, a theoretical error bound or deeper discussion of the slack introduced by these approximations is missing.

Active learning baselines: The active learning evaluation primarily compares against random and entropy-based heuristics; including competitive multimodal active learning baselines (such as core-set or submodular selection methods) would provide a more comprehensive picture.

strengths: Principled problem formulation: Applying Bayesian uncertainty quantification to pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) in a post-hoc, training-free manner without altering backbones is an important and timely topic.

Efficient and closed-form propagation: The paper derives closed-form approximations (ProbCosine) for the moments of cosine similarities between Gaussian-distributed feature embeddings, which allows uncertainty propagation through the probit approximation with negligible inference overhead (<1-5% relative runtime increase).

Comprehensive mathematical derivations: The appendix provides detailed derivations of the Kronecker-factored Generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) approximations and Jacobians for both InfoNCE and SigLIP loss functions.

Broad evaluation across settings: The method is validated across zero-shot classification, calibration evaluation, active learning with online Laplace updates (EPIG and BALD), and integration into existing probabilistic models (ProLIP, PCME++).
weaknesses: Marginal empirical advantage over simple baselines: While BayesVLM improves upon uncalibrated zero-shot CLIP, its performance gains over standard Temperature Scaling (a simple 1-parameter baseline) are very minor in NLPD and mixed across datasets, raising questions about whether the computational machinery of computing KFAC Hessians over large subsets of LAION is practically justified.

Degradation under pre-training data mismatch (SigLIP): As demonstrated in Table 9, when applied to SigLIP using LAION as proxy data, BayesVLM often increases Expected Calibration Error (ECE) compared to the vanilla model (e.g., ECE worsens on Flowers-102, Food-101, CIFAR-10, ImageNet-R). This exposes a significant practical limitation of requiring access to the exact pre-training distribution.

Heuristic nature of the moment approximations: The derivation of the expected cosine similarity in Equations (7), (8), and (52)–(61) relies on splitting $\mathbb{E}[A/B] \approx \mathbb{E}[A]/\mathbb{E}[B]$ and substituting an upper bound derived from the triangle inequality into the denominator. This lacks formal error bounds or second-order delta-method expansions to characterize the approximation error rigorously.

Uncertainty restricted to linear projection layers: Restricting the Laplace approximation solely to the final projection heads ($P$ and $Q$) ignores the epistemic uncertainty originating from the deep visual and textual transformer backbones, which constitute the vast majority of the network parameters.

Baselines in active learning: The active learning experiments compare BayesVLM acquisition functions primarily against naive heuristics (random, entropy). Comparisons against established active learning methods for transfer learning or foundation models (such as coreset-based or embedding diversity methods) are missing.
